title: GOD COMMANDED A PENALTY FOR SEX DURING MENSTRUATION—BUT THE REASON IS DEEPER THAN MOST CHRISTIANS REALIZE
paragraphs: GOD COMMANDED A PENALTY FOR SEX DURING MENSTRUATION—BUT THE REASON IS DEEPER THAN MOST CHRISTIANS REALIZE

Leviticus 20:18 contains one of the Bible’s most uncomfortable sexual laws. Was God condemning a woman’s natural body? Was this about impurity, holiness, or something far more serious? And what does this ancient command reveal about the grace of Jesus Christ? The answer may change the way you read Scripture—and the way you see people who have been made to feel unclean.
There is a verse in the Bible that many Christians have never heard preached from the pulpit.
Perhaps because it mentions blood.
Perhaps because it deals with sexual intimacy.

Or perhaps because explaining it properly requires us to confront something uncomfortable: the difference between what God actually said and what generations of religious people have assumed He meant.
The verse is Leviticus 20:18.
And before we go any further, imagine a woman sitting quietly in church.
She loves Jesus. She prays. She reads her Bible. But somewhere in her life, someone taught her that her monthly period made her dirty in God's eyes.
Maybe she was told she should not pray during menstruation.
Maybe she was made to feel ashamed of her body.
Maybe she grew up believing that the natural biological process God designed was somehow offensive to the God who designed her.
Then one day, she opens her Bible and discovers a law that seems to confirm everything she fears.
A man and a woman could be cut off from their people for sexual intercourse during menstruation.
She stops reading.
And the question rises in her heart:
God, why would You make my body this way and then call it unclean?
If that question has ever crossed your mind, or if you have struggled with difficult passages in the Old Testament, stay with me.
Because this is not merely a discussion about menstruation.
It is about holiness, covenant, human dignity, the danger of misunderstanding Scripture, and the Savior who refused to treat suffering people as untouchable.
And there is a moment in the Gospel of Mark that brings this entire conversation into astonishing focus.
But first, we must allow Leviticus to speak in its own historical and biblical context.
Leviticus 20:18 says in the King James Version:

"And if a man shall lie with a woman having her sickness, and shall uncover her nakedness; he hath discovered her fountain, and she hath uncovered the fountain of her blood: and both of them shall be cut off from among their people."
Those words sound severe because they are severe.
We should not soften them, pretend they are not there, or invent an explanation simply to make modern readers more comfortable.
But neither should we turn them into something the text never intended.
Notice something important.
The penalty was not imposed on a woman simply because she menstruated.
The verse addresses a particular prohibited sexual act involving a man and a woman. It names both participants, and it specifies the consequence within ancient Israel's covenant law.
That distinction matters enormously.
Menstruation itself was not presented as a moral crime.
To understand why, we need to go back to the original Hebrew.
The opening phrase reads:
וְאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר יִשְׁכַּב אֶת־אִשָּׁה דָּוָה
Ve'ish asher yishkav et-ishah davah.
A close rendering is:
"And a man who lies with a woman in her menstrual condition..."
The Hebrew verb yishkav, from שָׁכַב (shakhav), literally means "to lie down" and, in this context, refers to sexual intercourse.
The word דָּוָה (davah) refers here to a woman experiencing menstrual bleeding.
The passage continues with language about exposing or uncovering the "source" of her blood.
The Hebrew word מָקוֹר (maqor) means a source, spring, or fountain.
This is not the vocabulary of modern reproductive medicine. It is ancient Hebrew language describing bodily processes within Israel's laws of ritual purity and holiness.
And the final phrase contains another important expression:
וְנִכְרְתוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם מִקֶּרֶב עַמָּם
Venikhretu sheneihem miqqerev ammam.
"And both of them shall be cut off from among their people."
The Hebrew verb translated "cut off" comes from כָּרַת (karat), meaning "to cut."

In biblical law, being "cut off" is a serious covenant sanction. Its precise application is debated among interpreters; depending on the passage and interpretive tradition, it has been understood in terms of divine judgment, premature death, or exclusion from the covenant community.
We should therefore not confidently equate this phrase with a particular humanly administered punishment when Leviticus 20:18 does not specify one.
But the central message is unmistakable.
God treated this prohibition seriously within the covenant He established with Israel.
Why?
To understand that, we need to recognize a distinction that many believers have never been taught.
In the Old Testament, ritual uncleanness was not automatically the same thing as personal sin.
Read that again.
Because confusing those two categories has caused unnecessary shame, spiritual fear, and harmful religious teaching.
Leviticus 12 describes ritual impurity associated with childbirth.
Leviticus 15 addresses bodily discharges, including menstruation and male seminal emissions.
Numbers 19 discusses impurity resulting from contact with a dead body.
None of these circumstances necessarily means that someone has committed a moral offense.
A woman could give birth to a child without sinning by giving birth.
A man could experience a normal bodily emission without that event itself being a moral transgression.
A person could become ritually unclean through contact with death without having done anything wicked.
Ritual impurity described a condition affecting participation in certain aspects of Israel's worship and sacred life.
It was not simply another word for evil.
This distinction is essential.
Leviticus 15:19 says that when a woman experiences her regular menstrual discharge, she is in a state of ritual impurity for seven days.
The text does not command Israel to punish her for menstruating.
It does not say her character has become corrupt.
It does not declare that she is less valuable than a man.
Rather, it establishes regulations governing bodily discharges, contact, purification, and access to sacred space.
The Old Testament also addresses male bodily emissions, including in Leviticus 15:16–18.
So the biblical purity system was not simply a set of rules singling out women.
It was a larger system governing Israel's relationship with holiness, life, death, bodily conditions, and the presence of God.
Yet we must be careful here.
Not every detail of that system is fully explained in Scripture.
Some scholars emphasize the symbolic relationship between blood, life, mortality, and sacred boundaries.
Others highlight the distinction between ordinary bodily processes and the holiness required in Israel's sanctuary.
There are also discussions about the practical and social effects of these laws.
But Scripture does not explicitly say that Leviticus 20:18 was given primarily to prevent infection, protect reproductive health, or prevent sexual exploitation.
Those explanations may sound persuasive, but presenting them as God's stated reason would go beyond the evidence.
The strongest explanation must begin where the Bible itself begins: God's covenant holiness.
Leviticus 18:19 had already commanded:
"Also thou shalt not approach unto a woman to uncover her nakedness, as long as she is put apart for her uncleanness."
Leviticus 20:18 then states the covenant consequence for violating that prohibition.
And Ezekiel 18:6 includes the prohibition against approaching a menstruating woman among descriptions of righteous conduct.
These passages show that the command was not merely a rule about accidentally touching menstrual blood.
It addressed sexual intercourse during a specified period.

Leviticus 15:24 also describes ritual consequences when a man lies with a menstruating woman, while Leviticus 20:18 imposes a much more serious sanction. Interpreters have proposed distinctions involving intentional violation, knowledge, or the legal contexts of the passages, but the texts do not explain every difference.
We should acknowledge that tension rather than pretending it does not exist.
Now consider the larger context.
Leviticus 20:7–8 declares:
"Sanctify yourselves therefore, and be ye holy: for I am the LORD your God. And ye shall keep my statutes, and do them: I am the LORD which sanctify you."
The laws in this chapter form part of God's covenant instruction to Israel.
They teach that belonging to the Lord was not merely a matter of saying His name or attending religious gatherings.
Israel was called to reflect His holiness in worship, family relationships, sexual conduct, and community life.
Their bodies were not outside the scope of covenant obedience.
Their private choices were not disconnected from their public identity as God's people.
And their worship was not meant to be separated from the way they lived.
This is where the passage becomes personally challenging.
Because we live in a world that often tells us that whatever happens in private has nothing to do with God.
But Scripture consistently teaches that our bodies and our choices matter to Him.
That does not mean every regulation given to ancient Israel remains directly binding on Christians in precisely the same form.
It means we must take God's revelation seriously enough to understand both its original purpose and its place in the unfolding biblical story.
And that story is moving somewhere.
Toward a Person.
Toward a cross.
Toward Jesus Christ.
But before we arrive at Calvary, there is another woman we need to meet.
A woman whose story makes the subject of blood, impurity, and human dignity painfully personal.
She appears in Mark chapter 5.
We are not told her name.
We are told her suffering.
For twelve years, she had experienced a continuous flow of blood.
Twelve years.
Think about that.
Twelve years of waking up with a condition that would not disappear.
Twelve years of hoping the next treatment might finally work.
Twelve years of disappointment.
Mark 5:26 tells us that she had suffered under many physicians, spent everything she possessed, and grown worse rather than better.
Imagine spending your savings searching for relief.
Imagine exhausting your options.
Imagine the emotional weight of a condition that affects not only your physical health but also your participation in religious and social life.
Under the purity regulations of Leviticus 15:25–27, an abnormal ongoing discharge of blood placed a woman in a state of ritual impurity for as long as the discharge continued.
The Gospels do not tell us every detail of how her community treated her.
We should not invent a history of rejection that the text does not provide.
But the legal and social implications of prolonged impurity help us understand how difficult her circumstances could have been.
And then she heard about Jesus.
That is where everything began to change.
She did not approach Him with a theological argument.
She did not come carrying a record of religious accomplishments.
She came desperate.
Perhaps exhausted.
Certainly in need of healing.
Mark 5:27–28 says:
"When she had heard of Jesus, came in the press behind, and touched his garment. For she said, If I may touch but his clothes, I shall be whole."
Can you picture it?
The crowd pressing against Jesus.
People moving in every direction.
Voices everywhere.
And one suffering woman reaching through the confusion.
Not asking for applause.
Not seeking attention.
Just reaching.
One touch.
That was all she wanted.
And immediately, according to Mark 5:29, the flow of her blood stopped.
Twelve years of suffering.
And in a moment, her body was healed.
But the story does not end with the miracle.
Jesus stopped.
He asked who had touched His clothes.
The disciples were confused because the crowd was pressing against Him.
But Jesus knew that power had gone out from Him.
And the woman, trembling with fear, came forward and told Him the truth.
Here is the moment that should silence every voice that has ever used Scripture to make a suffering woman feel worthless.
Jesus did not humiliate her.
He did not announce that her body made her disgusting.
He did not reduce her identity to her condition.
He spoke to her.
And Mark 5:34 records His words:
"Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace, and be whole of thy plague."
Daughter.
Not an embarrassment.
Not a burden.
Not a problem to be avoided.
Daughter.
The Greek word is θυγάτηρ (thygatēr).
It means "daughter."
It is a deeply personal form of address.
And Jesus used it for a woman whose suffering had defined twelve years of her life.
Do not miss the significance.
The woman had approached Him seeking physical healing.
Jesus publicly acknowledged her faith and sent her away in peace.
Her condition did not make her unworthy of His compassion.
Her suffering did not disqualify her from approaching Him.
And His holiness was not diminished by her need.
Now, we must interpret this carefully.
The woman in Mark 5 had a prolonged abnormal discharge, not simply an ordinary monthly period.
Her story does not directly repeal Leviticus 20:18, nor is it an account of the prohibited sexual act described there.
But it reveals something essential about the character and ministry of Jesus.
The Savior who perfectly embodied God's holiness did not treat a ritually unclean sufferer as someone beyond His mercy.
That matters.
Especially for anyone who has confused being ceremonially unclean under ancient Israel's law with being spiritually worthless before God.
Jesus did not come to teach people that holiness was meaningless.
He came to fulfill the Law and the Prophets.
Matthew 5:17 records His words:
"Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil."
That statement changes how Christians must approach Leviticus.
We cannot simply tear difficult verses out of the Old Testament and act as though they never existed.
But neither can we take every regulation of Israel's covenant system and impose it directly on believers without considering the fulfillment accomplished through Christ.
The New Testament explains that Jesus' death, resurrection, and priestly ministry inaugurated the new covenant.
Hebrews 9–10 describes the limitations of the former sacrificial system and the sufficiency of Christ's offering.
Hebrews 10:10 declares:
"By the which will we are sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all."
Once for all.
Those words are extraordinary.
Because the story of Scripture is not ultimately about human beings discovering enough rituals to make themselves acceptable.
It is about the holy God who provides redemption through His Son.
The Old Testament purity system taught Israel to take holiness seriously.
But the New Testament reveals the decisive cleansing accomplished by Jesus Christ.
In Mark 7:20–23, Jesus teaches that moral defilement is rooted in the human heart, from which evil thoughts and sinful actions proceed.
In Acts 15, the apostles address the obligations of Gentile believers without requiring them to adopt the entire Mosaic covenant system.
And in Galatians, Paul warns against making observance of the Mosaic Law the basis of justification before God.
Christians therefore do not ordinarily treat the menstrual purity regulations of Leviticus as binding ceremonial requirements under the new covenant.
At the same time, Christians continue to be called to sexual holiness, faithfulness, love, and self-control.
The New Testament does not give a direct, explicit command repeating Leviticus 20:18's specific prohibition or its covenant penalty for Christians.
That is important to say plainly.
It would be misleading to claim that the New Testament commands churches to impose the ancient penalty on couples who have intercourse during menstruation.
It does not.

Christians may hold different personal convictions about intimacy during menstruation, and married couples should approach such decisions with mutual respect, care, consent, and consideration for health and comfort.
But we should not turn a disputed application of ancient covenant law into a universal New Testament command without biblical warrant.
And we should never use this passage to shame a woman for menstruating.
The Bible does not teach that a woman's monthly period makes her less loved by God.
It does not make her prayers worthless.
It does not make her incapable of worshiping Jesus.
It does not make her spiritually inferior to her husband.
And it does not place her outside the reach of Christ's grace.
The God who formed the human body is not surprised by the body He formed.
Psalm 139:13–14 speaks of God's intimate knowledge of our formation.
The body is not an accidental mistake.
And the Gospel does not ask women to despise their humanity in order to be loved by their Creator.
But there is another truth we must not overlook.
Grace is not permission to disregard everything God calls holy.
Some people read difficult Old Testament laws and conclude that God's standards must have been cruel.
Others read the New Testament and conclude that because Jesus forgives, holiness no longer matters.
Both conclusions fail to appreciate the full biblical story.
The same Jesus who welcomed sinners also called people to repentance.
The same Savior who showed compassion also confronted hypocrisy.
The same Christ who offered forgiveness also taught His disciples to deny themselves and follow Him.
Grace is not God's declaration that sin never mattered.
Grace is God's merciful answer to sinners who could never save themselves.
And that answer came at an immeasurable cost.
The cross.
Consider the contrast.
Leviticus speaks repeatedly about blood, purity, sacrifice, and access to the presence of God.
The New Testament announces that Christ has opened the way to God through His own sacrificial death.
First Peter 1:18–19 says that believers were redeemed not with corruptible things such as silver and gold, but with the precious blood of Christ.
And Hebrews 9:14 asks how much more the blood of Christ will cleanse our consciences from dead works to serve the living God.
This does not mean menstrual blood and Christ's sacrificial blood are identical categories.
They are not.
Nor does it mean every menstrual regulation in Leviticus was a direct prophecy of Jesus.
We must resist forcing symbolism onto Scripture.
But the broader biblical movement is unmistakable.

From a covenant system in which purity and access to sacred space were carefully regulated, the New Testament brings us to the Messiah through whom sinners receive cleansing, forgiveness, and access to the Father.
And suddenly, the most important question is no longer merely:
"Why was there a penalty in Leviticus 20:18?"
The deeper question becomes:
"What has Jesus Christ accomplished that changes how we approach God?"
Because every one of us knows something about feeling unclean.
Perhaps not ceremonially.
Perhaps not physically.
But morally.
Spiritually.
Emotionally.
There are people reading this who carry memories they have never spoken aloud.
A relationship that crossed boundaries.
A private habit that became a prison.
A betrayal.
An abortion.
Sexual sin.
A secret addiction.
A marriage wounded by unfaithfulness.
A season of rebellion that still haunts the conscience.
Or perhaps your burden is different.
You were not the person who committed the wrong.
You were the person who was hurt.
Someone violated your trust.
Someone manipulated you.
Someone made you feel that what happened to you destroyed your worth.
And years later, you still struggle to believe that you can stand before God without shame.
Hear this carefully.
Being sinned against is not the same as committing sin.
The evil another person inflicted upon you does not make you morally guilty for their actions.
And whether you need forgiveness for what you have done or healing from what has been done to you, Jesus Christ is not indifferent to your pain.
He sees.
He knows.
He calls people to truth.
And He offers mercy.
First John 1:9 declares:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
Not some unrighteousness.
All unrighteousness.
That promise does not erase the need for repentance, accountability, restitution where appropriate, or the real consequences of wrongdoing.
But it announces something greater than our ability to repair ourselves.
God forgives those who come to Him through Christ.
And the Gospel does not end with forgiveness alone.
It calls us into a transformed life.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's grace trains believers to renounce ungodliness and live upright, godly lives.
Grace does not merely comfort us while leaving us unchanged.
Grace teaches us to walk differently.
To love differently.
To treat our bodies and other people's bodies with dignity.
To stop confusing religious shame with biblical holiness.
To stop excusing genuine sin while condemning innocent bodily processes.
To stop using difficult verses as weapons against people Jesus calls us to love.
And to begin reading Scripture with reverence, humility, and a willingness to be corrected.
Maybe that is what this passage is asking of us today.
Not that we invent a modern penalty.
Not that we condemn women for menstruation.
Not that we dismiss the Old Testament as irrelevant.
But that we learn to distinguish covenant law, ritual impurity, moral wrongdoing, and the fulfillment of God's redemptive purposes in Christ.
Because when we fail to make those distinctions, people get hurt.
Women can be burdened with shame God never commanded.
Couples can be taught rules as divine commands without sufficient biblical support.
Believers can become frightened of their own bodies.
And skeptics can be given the impression that Christianity has no serious way to interpret its own Scriptures.
But when we read faithfully, something beautiful happens.
We discover that God's holiness is not opposed to His mercy.
His mercy does not cancel His holiness.
And Jesus Christ reveals both with perfect clarity.
Remember the woman in the crowd.
Twelve years of bleeding.
Twelve years of searching.
One encounter with Jesus.
And one word that restored her dignity in the hearing of everyone around her.
Daughter.
Maybe that is the word someone needed to hear today.
Not because the Bible promises that every illness will disappear immediately.
Not because faith guarantees a painless life.
But because suffering does not erase a person's value before God.
And no one who comes to Christ in genuine faith needs to imagine that His compassion is reserved only for people with spotless histories and uncomplicated bodies.
Perhaps you have spent years trying to hide the parts of your story that embarrass you.
Perhaps you know the Bible's commands but have forgotten the tenderness of its Savior.
Perhaps you have been calling yourself dirty when God is calling you to understand His Word more faithfully.
Or perhaps you have been calling something harmless that Scripture genuinely identifies as sin, and today the Holy Spirit is convicting you to repent.
Whatever your situation, do not run from the truth.
Run toward Jesus.
Because truth without compassion can become a weapon in human hands.
And compassion without truth can become an excuse to remain unchanged.
But in Jesus Christ, grace and truth meet.
John 1:17 says:
"For the law was given by Moses, but grace and truth came by Jesus Christ."
The Gospel is not the story of God abandoning holiness.
It is the story of the holy God rescuing sinners through the life, death, and resurrection of His Son.
That is why our message will always be:
Not because every scandal is automatically redeemed without repentance.
Not because consequences disappear.
Not because grace makes evil good.
But because Jesus can forgive real sin, restore broken lives, heal wounded hearts, and write a new future for those who turn to Him.
And if this article challenged something you believed about menstruation, holiness, or the Old Testament, I want to hear from you.
Not a rehearsed religious answer.
An honest one.
What affected you most: discovering that ritual uncleanness was not necessarily personal sin, or seeing how Jesus treated the woman who suffered for twelve years?
If you have been carrying unnecessary shame, you can simply comment, "Christ is still healing me."
If this passage has exposed something in your life that genuinely requires repentance, you can comment, "Jesus, teach me to walk in truth."
You do not need to disclose private experiences or painful details publicly. Your honesty matters more than how much you reveal.
And please do not let this truth stop with you.
Not merely because sharing helps our ministry reach more people—although it genuinely can.
Somewhere there may be a husband who needs to understand Scripture more carefully.
Somewhere there may be a young Christian struggling with a difficult verse and wondering whether the Bible can be trusted.
And somewhere there may be an unbeliever who has never seen Christians approach a controversial biblical passage with both conviction and compassion.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, spiritual seekers, and even those who have walked away from church to follow along.
We want people to encounter the Gospel—not simply religious arguments, but the living truth of Christ.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not be done grudgingly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not guilt.
Not pressure.
Gratitude.
Shared mission.
A desire to see more people encounter the truth of Jesus Christ.
Because our goal is not merely to attract readers.
It is to help people open their Bibles, understand the truth, repent where repentance is needed, receive the grace of Christ, and grow into faithful disciples.
And now, as we come to the end, remember where we began.
With a difficult verse.
A severe ancient penalty.
A question about blood.
A woman who might have wondered whether God considered her body shameful.
And then we encountered another woman.
A woman who had suffered for twelve years.
Who reached toward Jesus.
Who was healed.
And who heard the Savior call her "Daughter."
That does not erase the seriousness of Leviticus 20:18.
The story of a holy God.
A covenant people.
A world wounded by sin.
And a Savior who came not to make sin insignificant, but to redeem sinners and bring them near to God.
So the next time someone tells you that your natural bodily processes make you spiritually worthless, remember what Scripture actually teaches.
And the next time someone tells you that grace means holiness no longer matters, remember the cross.
Because Jesus did not shed His blood to teach us that sin is harmless.
He gave Himself to redeem us from it.
And if you remember only one thing from this entire article, remember this:
The blood that marked a woman's suffering did not make her unworthy of Jesus—and the blood Christ shed at Calvary is sufficient to cleanse every repentant sinner who comes to Him in faith.
